## Introduction

In this assignment, we explore the Seoul Bike Sharing dataset and develop multiple 
linear regression models to predict daily bicycle rentals.

We begin by importing and exploring the data, then prepare the data for modeling, 
fit three regression models, and compare their predictive performance using RMSE.

## Reading in the Data

```{r}
# Load the packages needed for data manipulation and exploration
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(rsample)

# Read the locally saved Seoul Bike Sharing dataset
# Specify Latin1 encoding to handle special characters
bike_data <- read_csv(
  "data/SeoulBikeData.csv",
  locale = locale(encoding = "Latin1")
)
```


## Exploratory data analysis

### 1) Checking for missing values

```{r}
# Count missing values in each column
colSums(is.na(bike_data))
```
There are no missing values in the data.

### 2) Check column types and values within the columns
```{r}
# Examine the structure of the dataset
# glimpse() tells us the number of rows, columns, variable names, data types, and 
#sample values
glimpse(bike_data)

# head() lets us see the first six observations
head(bike_data)

# provides min, max, quartiles, median and mean for numeric variables
summary(bike_data)

# unique() lets us inspect the unique values of the categorical variables.
unique(bike_data$Seasons)
unique(bike_data$Holiday)
unique(bike_data$"Functioning Day")
```

We have 8,760 observations across 14 variables (columns). Of these 10 are numeric 
and 4 are character variables. Three of the character variables are categorical 
(`Seasons`, `Holiday`, ` Functioning Day`) while the `Date` variable needs to be 
converted to the proper date format. 

Each observation represents one hour of bike rental activity, rather than an individual 
rental. The `Hour` variable identifies the hour of the day (0–23), while `Rented Bike Count` 
represents the number of bikes rented during that hour. The dataset covers 365 days, 
with 24 hourly observations per day, so there are a total of 8,760 observations. 


### 3) Convert `Date' column to actual date format

```{r}

# Convert Date from character to Date format (day/month/year)
# Use dmy() function from the lubridate package
bike_data$Date <- dmy(bike_data$Date)

# confirm conversion
class(bike_data$Date)
```
### 4) Convert the character variables into factors using factor()

After converting the character variables to factors using the `factor()` function, 
we used the `levels` function to identify the unique values for each one.
```{r}
# Convert Seasons from character to factor
bike_data$Seasons <- factor(bike_data$Seasons)
# Display the factor's levels
levels(bike_data$Seasons)

# Convert Holiday from character to factor
bike_data$Holiday <- factor(bike_data$Holiday)
# Display the factor's levels
levels(bike_data$Holiday)

# Convert Functioning Day from character to factor
bike_data$"Functioning Day" <- factor(bike_data$"Functioning Day")
# Display the factor's levels
levels(bike_data$"Functioning Day")
```


### 5) Rename variables

```{r}
# Rename variables using lower snake case for easier reference
bike_data <- bike_data |>
  rename(
    date = Date,
    bike_count = `Rented Bike Count`,
    hour = Hour,
    temp = `Temperature(°C)`,
    humidity = `Humidity(%)`,
    wind_speed = `Wind speed (m/s)`,
    visibility = `Visibility (10m)`,
    dew_point_temp = `Dew point temperature(°C)`, # backticks are needed because of spaces in original name
    solar_radiation = `Solar Radiation (MJ/m2)`,
    rainfall = `Rainfall(mm)`,
    snowfall = `Snowfall (cm)`,
    seasons = Seasons,
    holiday = Holiday,
    functioning_day = `Functioning Day`
  )

# Verify the new column names
names(bike_data)
```

### 6) Create summary statistics

#### - Numeric variables

```{r}
# Generate summary statistics for all numerical variables
bike_data |>
  select(where(is.numeric)) |>
  summary()
```

#### - Categorical variables

##### + Seasons
```{r}
# Calculate summary statistics for hourly bike rentals by season
bike_data |>
  group_by(seasons) |>
  summarise(
    observations = n(),
    mean_rentals = mean(bike_count),
    median_rentals = median(bike_count),
    total_rentals = sum(bike_count)
  )
```
We grouped the observations by season to examine differences in hourly bike rentals. 
Summer had the highest average, with approximately 1,034 rentals per hour, followed 
by autumn (820), spring (730), and winter (226). Total rentals were also highest during 
summer, at about 2.28 million, compared with just 487,000 during winter. These 
results suggest strong seasonality in bike rental activity, with much higher demand 
during warmer months.


##### + Holidays
```{r}
# Calculate summary statistics for hourly bike rentals by holiday status
bike_data |>
  group_by(holiday) |>
  summarise(
    observations = n(),
    mean_rentals = mean(bike_count),
    median_rentals = median(bike_count),
    total_rentals = sum(bike_count)
  )
```
We also examined hourly bike rentals based on whether a day was classified as a `holiday`. 
Non-holidays averaged approximately 715 rentals per hour, compared with 500 on holidays. 
Median rentals were also considerably higher on non-holidays (524.5) than on holidays (240). 
This suggests that bike rental activity tends to be lower during holidays. However, there 
were substantially fewer holiday observations (432) than non-holiday observations (8,328), 
so comparing hourly averages is more informative than comparing total rentals.

##### + Functioning day
```{r}
# Calculate summary statistics for hourly bike rentals by functioning day
bike_data |>
  group_by(functioning_day) |>
  summarise(
    observations = n(),
    mean_rentals = mean(bike_count),
    median_rentals = median(bike_count),
    total_rentals = sum(bike_count)
  )
```

Next we examined bike rental activity based on whether the bike-sharing system was 
functioning. Of the 8,760 hourly observations, 295 were classified as non-functioning, 
and all recorded zero rentals. During functioning periods, the system averaged 
approximately 729 rentals per hour, with a median of 542 and a total of approximately 
6.17 million rentals.

Because the zero rentals during non-functioning periods reflect the system being 
unavailable rather than necessarily indicating a lack of demand, we have decided to 
exclude these observations from our analysis. This leaves 8,465 hourly observations for 
the next stage.

```{r}
# Excluding nonfunctioning hourly observations from the dataset 
bike_data <- bike_data |>
  filter(functioning_day == "Yes")

# Verify the number of remaining observations
nrow(bike_data)
```
### 7) Converting to daily dataset

To simplify the remaining analysis we aggregate hourly observations into daily totals.
```{r}
# Aggregate hourly observations into daily observations
bike_daily <- bike_data |>
  group_by(date, seasons, holiday) |> # group_by() organizes observations into desired groups
  summarise(
    # Calculate daily totals
    bike_count = sum(bike_count),
    rainfall = sum(rainfall),
    snowfall = sum(snowfall), 

    # Calculate daily averages for weather variables
    temp = mean(temp),
    humidity = mean(humidity),
    wind_speed = mean(wind_speed),
    visibility = mean(visibility),
    dew_point_temp = mean(dew_point_temp),
    solar_radiation = mean(solar_radiation),

    # Remove grouping after summarizing
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Check whether our daily dataset is still grouped
group_vars(bike_daily)

# Inspect the new daily dataset
glimpse(bike_daily)

```
Hourly observations were aggregated into a new daily dataset called `bike_daily` by 
grouping the data by date, season, and holiday status. We then calculated daily totals 
for bike rentals, rainfall, and snowfall, while taking the average of the remaining 
weather variables. After excluding nonfunctioning hours (295 hrs = 24 x 12 non-functioning 
days + 7 additional hours during functioning days), the resulting dataset contains
**353 daily observations across 12 variables**, compared with the original 8,760 hourly 
observations across 14 variables. This daily dataset will be used for the remainder 
of our analysis.

### 8) Summarizing daily stats


#### - Numeric variables
```{r}
# Generate summary statistics for our daily dataset
summary(bike_daily)
```
The daily dataset now contains 353 observations, with an average of 17,485 bike rentals 
per day. Daily rentals ranged from a minimum of 977 to a maximum of 36,149. The median 
of 18,563 is slightly higher than the mean, suggesting that some lower-rental days may 
be pulling the average down. The dataset includes 17 holidays and 336 non-holidays. The 
weather variables are also summarized.


#### - Categorical variables

##### + Seasons
```{r}
# Calculate summary statistics for daily bike rentals by season
bike_daily |>
  group_by(seasons) |>
  summarise(
    days = n(),
    mean_rentals = mean(bike_count),
    median_rentals = median(bike_count),
    total_rentals = sum(bike_count)
  )
```
##### + Holidays
```{r}
# Calculate summary statistics for daily bike rentals by holiday status
bike_daily |>
  group_by(holiday) |>
  summarise(
    days = n(),
    mean_rentals = mean(bike_count),
    median_rentals = median(bike_count),
    total_rentals = sum(bike_count)
  )
```
Next we calculated summary statistics for daily bike rentals by season and holiday 
status. 

Summer had the highest average with approximately 24,818 rentals per day, followed by 
autumn (22,099), spring (17,910), and winter (5,413). This suggests strong seasonality 
with substantially fewer rentals as the months get colder.

We also found that bike rentals were lower on holidays, averaging about 12,700 per 
day compared with 17,727 on non-holidays. The number of holiday observations was 
relatively small (17 days), compared with 336 non-holidays.

#### - Graphical summaries

##### + Boxplots
```{r}
# Compare the distribution of daily bike rentals across seasons
ggplot(bike_daily, aes(x = seasons, y = bike_count)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Daily Bike Rentals by Season",
    x = "Season",
    y = "Daily Bike Rentals"
  )

# Compare the distribution of daily bike rentals on holidays and non-holidays
ggplot(bike_daily, aes(x = holiday, y = bike_count)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Daily Bike Rentals by Holiday Status",
    x = "Holiday Status",
    y = "Daily Bike Rentals"
  )

```

The boxplots confirm bike rentals vary considerably by season and holiday status, 
consistent with the differences observed in our summary statistics above. 

Summer has the highest median rentals, followed by autumn, spring, and winter. We 
notice that winter has a noticeably smaller spread, while summer has a few unusually 
low observations.

The holiday boxplot also shows that median daily rentals are much lower on holidays 
than on non-holidays. That said, it does appear that both groups have substantial 
variation. 

##### + Scatterplots
```{r}
# Select all numerical variables from our daily dataset
bike_numeric <- bike_daily |>
  select(where(is.numeric))

# Create a scatterplot matrix using all numerical variables
# Display only the upper triangle to avoid duplicate plots
pairs(
  bike_numeric,
  lower.panel = NULL,
  main = "Scatterplot Matrix of Daily Bike Variables",
  pch = 16,
  cex = 0.3
)
```
##### + Correlation matrix and heat map
```{r}
# Select all numerical variables from our daily dataset
bike_numeric <- bike_daily |>
  select(where(is.numeric))

# Calculate the correlation matrix
cor_matrix <- cor(bike_numeric)

# Display the correlations rounded to two decimal places
round(cor_matrix, 2)

# Convert correlation matrix to a data frame
cor_data <- as.data.frame(as.table(cor_matrix))

# Set the variable order to match the scatterplot matrix
var_order <- colnames(cor_matrix)

cor_data$Var1 <- factor(cor_data$Var1, levels = var_order)
cor_data$Var2 <- factor(cor_data$Var2, levels = var_order)

# Keep only the upper-right triangle, including the diagonal
cor_data <- cor_data |>
  filter(as.numeric(Var1) <= as.numeric(Var2))

# Create the heatmap
ggplot(cor_data, aes(x = Var2, y = Var1, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev(var_order)) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "yellow",
    mid = "orange",
    high = "red",
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(-1, 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Correlation Heatmap of Daily Bike Variables",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Correlation"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
)

```
The correlation matrix measures helps us understand the linear relationship, or lack thereof, 
between all the numerical variables. To further illustrate we use a scatterplot matrix  
and correlation heatmap. Since the relationships are mirrored, we displayed only 
the upper-right half of the matrix. Important to note that a scatterplot also helps us 
identify non-linear relationships. 

Bike rentals have relatively strong positive correlations with temperature (0.75), 
solar radiation (0.74), and dew point temperature (0.65). Rainfall (-0.24) and snowfall 
(-0.27) have weaker negative correlations, while humidity (0.04) shows almost no 
linear relationship with bike rentals.

We also notice a very strong correlation between temperature and dew point temperature 
(0.96), suggesting potential multicollinearity in our regression models. The scatterplots 
also suggest that some relationships, particularly between bike rentals and temperature, 
may not be entirely linear.
